problems.html: Let A=(4213)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}A=(41​23​). Verify that u=(21)\mathbf{u}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}u=(21​) and w=(1−1)\mathbf{w}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}w=(1−1​) are eigenvectors, and state the eigenvalue of each. Check your two eigenvalues against trA\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf{A}trA and det⁡A\det\mathbf{A}detA.
hints: You are not solving anything here — just multiplying. Work out Au\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}Au and Aw\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w}Aw, and compare each with its own vector.
If Au\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}Au comes out as a multiple of u\mathbf{u}u, that multiple is itself the eigenvalue. Read it straight off.

problems.html: Let A=(2112)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}A=(21​12​). (a) Write down the characteristic equation and solve it for the eigenvalues. (b) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue.
hints: The characteristic equation is det⁡(A−λI)=0\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0det(A−λI)=0. Write down A−λI\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I}A−λI first; for a 2×22\times22×2 the determinant is ad−bcad-bcad−bc.
You should reach (2−λ)2−1=0(2-\lambda)^2-1=0(2−λ)2−1=0. Treat it as a difference of two squares and factorise: two factors, so two eigenvalues.

For (b), take one eigenvalue at a time and solve (A−λI)v=0(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}(A−λI)v=0. Both rows say the same thing, which is why an eigenvector is only fixed up to scale.
problems.format: λs smaller first; each v's 2nd entry (1st = 1)

problems.html: (a) Find the eigenvalues of the quarter-turn R=(0−110)\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}R=(01​−10​). (b) Using R(θ)=(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ)\mathbf{R}(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}R(θ)=(cosθsinθ​−sinθcosθ​), write down the eigenvalues of the 60∘60^\circ60∘ rotation.
hints: Set up det⁡(R−λI)=0\det(\mathbf{R}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0det(R−λI)=0 as usual; do not be put off when it has no real root.
The determinant is (−λ)(−λ)−(−1)(1)(-\lambda)(-\lambda)-(-1)(1)(−λ)(−λ)−(−1)(1). Simplify it and solve; the roots are the numbers Unit 3 introduced.

For (b), the characteristic equation of R(θ)\mathbf{R}(\theta)R(θ) is λ2−2λcos⁡θ+1=0\lambda^2-2\lambda\cos\theta+1=0λ2−2λcosθ+1=0; the quadratic formula and cos⁡2θ−1=−sin⁡2θ\cos^2\theta-1=-\sin^2\thetacos2θ−1=−sin2θ take it from there. The box wants only the pair from (a): check that it adds to tr⁡R\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{R}trR and multiplies to det⁡R\det\mathbf{R}detR.
problems.format: the eigenvalues of R in (a); +i first

problems.html: (a) For each matrix say whether it is symmetric, Hermitian, both, or neither: (i) (1225),(ii) (2i−i3),(iii) (03−30),(iv) (12+i2+i4).\text{(i)}\ \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&5\end{pmatrix},\quad\allowbreak \text{(ii)}\ \begin{pmatrix}2&\mathrm{i}\\-\mathrm{i}&3\end{pmatrix},\quad\allowbreak \text{(iii)}\ \begin{pmatrix}0&3\\-3&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\allowbreak \text{(iv)}\ \begin{pmatrix}1&2+\mathrm{i}\\2+\mathrm{i}&4\end{pmatrix}.(i) (12​25​),(ii) (2−i​i3​),(iii) (0−3​30​),(iv) (12+i​2+i4​). (b) For u=(1,i)T\mathbf{u}=(1,\mathrm{i})^{\mathsf{T}}u=(1,i)T and w=(i,1)T\mathbf{w}=(\mathrm{i},1)^{\mathsf{T}}w=(i,1)T compute the conjugate inner product u†w=u1‾w1+u2‾w2\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{w}=\overline{u_1}w_1+\overline{u_2}w_2u†w=u1​​w1​+u2​​w2​ and the plain product uTw\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{w}uTw. Are u\mathbf{u}u and w\mathbf{w}w orthogonal?
hints: Symmetric means AT=A\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{A}AT=A; Hermitian means A‾T=A\overline{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{A}AT=A (transpose and conjugate). For a real matrix the two coincide.
Check the diagonal and the off-diagonal pair: a Hermitian matrix has real diagonal entries, and its off-diagonal entries are conjugates of each other, not equal.
For (b), the conjugate inner product conjugates the entries of u\mathbf{u}u before multiplying: i‾=−i\overline{\mathrm{i}}=-\mathrm{i}i=−i. The plain product skips that step.

problems.html: Decide, with a one-line reason, whether each matrix is diagonalisable: (a) (1203),(b) (3103),(c) (2002).\text{(a)}\ \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.(a) (10​23​),(b) (30​13​),(c) (20​02​).
hints: Two distinct eigenvalues in a 2×22\times22×2 matrix is already enough to guarantee diagonalisability. Which of these have that?
When an eigenvalue is repeated you must go further and count independent eigenvectors: solve (A−λI)v=0(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}(A−λI)v=0 and count the free unknowns.
A repeated eigenvalue with only one independent eigenvector is defective, and the matrix is not diagonalisable.

problems.html: A 2×22\times22×2 matrix A\mathbf{A}A has eigenpairs λ1=3, v1=(1,1)T\lambda_1=3,\ \mathbf{v}_1=(1,1)^{\mathsf{T}}λ1​=3, v1​=(1,1)T and λ2=−2, v2=(1,−1)T\lambda_2=-2,\ \mathbf{v}_2=(1,-1)^{\mathsf{T}}λ2​=−2, v2​=(1,−1)T. (a) Write down matrices P\mathbf{P}P and D\mathbf{D}D with A=PDP−1\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{P}^{-1}A=PDP−1, and compute P−1\mathbf{P}^{-1}P−1. (b) Write down D5\mathbf{D}^{5}D5 and Dk\mathbf{D}^{k}Dk for a general positive integer kkk.
hints: The eigenvectors are the columns of P\mathbf{P}P, in the same order as the eigenvalues down the diagonal of D\mathbf{D}D.
For P−1\mathbf{P}^{-1}P−1 use the 2×22\times22×2 formula: swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal ones, divide by det⁡P\det\mathbf{P}detP.
For (b), powers of a diagonal matrix act entry by entry, and (−2)5(-2)^5(−2)5 is negative.
problems.format: P⁻¹ row by row (decimals); D⁵ diagonal

problems.html: A transition matrix has non-negative entries and columns that sum to one. (a) Which of these qualify? (i) (0.60.10.40.9),(ii) (0.50.50.50.6),(iii) (0.30.70.70.3).\text{(i)}\ \begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.1\\0.4&0.9\end{pmatrix},\quad\allowbreak \text{(ii)}\ \begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.5\\0.5&0.6\end{pmatrix},\quad\allowbreak \text{(iii)}\ \begin{pmatrix}0.3&0.7\\0.7&0.3\end{pmatrix}.(i) (0.60.4​0.10.9​),(ii) (0.50.5​0.50.6​),(iii) (0.30.7​0.70.3​). (b) Find the steady-state distribution of matrix (i): the eigenvector for λ=1\lambda=1λ=1, scaled so its entries sum to one.
hints: Two conditions must hold together: every entry ≥0\geq0≥0, and each column (not each row) summing to exactly 111.
For (b) solve (P−I)x=0(\mathbf{P}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}(P−I)x=0 for matrix (i); both rows give the same condition relating x1x_1x1​ and x2x_2x2​.
A distribution must sum to 111: scale the direction you found by the sum of its entries. Check with Px∞=x∞\mathbf{P}\mathbf{x}_\infty=\mathbf{x}_\inftyPx∞​=x∞​.

problems.html: For A=(4123)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}A=(42​13​) find the eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each, and verify the trace/determinant identities.
hints: Form det⁡(A−λI)=0\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0det(A−λI)=0: it becomes (4−λ)(3−λ)−2=0(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2=0(4−λ)(3−λ)−2=0.
Expand to λ2−7λ+10=0\lambda^2-7\lambda+10=0λ2−7λ+10=0 and factorise.
The check you want: the eigenvalues should add to the trace 777 and multiply to the determinant 101010.

problems.html: Let A=(1221)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}A=(12​21​). (a) Diagonalise A=PDP−1\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{P}^{-1}A=PDP−1. (b) Hence derive a closed form for Ak\mathbf{A}^{k}Ak, valid for every positive integer kkk. (c) Check your formula at k=1k=1k=1.
hints: Eigenvalues first: the characteristic equation is (1−λ)2−4=0(1-\lambda)^2-4=0(1−λ)2−4=0, a difference of two squares. Factorise it.
Build P\mathbf{P}P from the eigenvectors and D\mathbf{D}D from the eigenvalues, keeping the order consistent.

For part (b) use Ak=PDkP−1\mathbf{A}^k=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^k\mathbf{P}^{-1}Ak=PDkP−1 — and Dk\mathbf{D}^kDk is easy because D\mathbf{D}D is diagonal. The box wants only the eigenvalues from (a): check that they add to tr⁡A\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{A}trA and multiply to det⁡A\det\mathbf{A}detA.

problems.html: A sequence satisfies xn+1=xn+2xn−1x_{n+1}=x_n+2x_{n-1}xn+1​=xn​+2xn−1​ with x0=0, x1=1x_0=0,\ x_1=1x0​=0, x1​=1 (giving 0,1,1,3,5,11,…0,1,1,3,5,11,\dots0,1,1,3,5,11,…). (a) Write the step as (xn+1xn)=A(xnxn−1)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_{n+1}\\x_n\end{smallmatrix}\right) =\mathbf{A}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_{n}\\x_{n-1}\end{smallmatrix}\right)(xn+1​xn​​)=A(xn​xn−1​​) and find A\mathbf{A}A and its eigenvalues. (b) Decompose the start vector in the eigenbasis and obtain a closed form for xnx_nxn​.
hints: A recurrence that reaches two steps back becomes a one-step matrix recurrence once you carry both terms in the vector.
The first row of A\mathbf{A}A must reproduce the recurrence itself; the second row only has to copy xnx_nxn​ from the top of the old vector to the bottom of the new one.

For (b), write the start vector as a combination of the two eigenvectors. Each one is then scaled by its own eigenvalue to the nnn-th power, and the second component of the result is xnx_nxn​. Evaluate your closed form at n=10n=10n=10.
problems.format: the eigenvalues, larger first; then x₁₀

problems.html: Let H=(32i−2i3)\mathbf{H}=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 2\mathrm{i}\\ -2\mathrm{i}& 3\end{pmatrix}H=(3−2i​2i3​). (a) Confirm H\mathbf{H}H is Hermitian. (b) Find its eigenvalues (they should be real) and an eigenvector for each. (c) Verify the two eigenvectors are orthogonal under the conjugate inner product u†v=u1‾v1+u2‾v2\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{v}=\overline{u_1}v_1+\overline{u_2}v_2u†v=u1​​v1​+u2​​v2​.
hints: Hermitian means the conjugate transpose returns the matrix: transpose it and conjugate every entry, then compare.
For the eigenvalues, note (2i)(−2i)=−4i2=4(2\mathrm{i})(-2\mathrm{i})=-4\mathrm{i}^2=4(2i)(−2i)=−4i2=4, so the characteristic equation is (3−λ)2−4=0(3-\lambda)^2-4=0(3−λ)2−4=0.

For (c), the conjugate inner product conjugates the entries of the first vector before multiplying; the plain dot product would mislead. For the box, check your two eigenvalues: both real, adding to tr⁡H\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{H}trH and multiplying to det⁡H\det\mathbf{H}detH.

problems.html: The symmetric matrix A=(31−113−1−1−15)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}3&1&-1\\1&3&-1\\-1&-1&5\end{pmatrix}A=​31−1​13−1​−1−15​​ has eigenvalues λ=2,3,6\lambda=2,3,6λ=2,3,6, with eigenvectors (1,−1,0)T(1,-1,0)^{\mathsf{T}}(1,−1,0)T, (1,1,1)T(1,1,1)^{\mathsf{T}}(1,1,1)T, (1,1,−2)T(1,1,-2)^{\mathsf{T}}(1,1,−2)T respectively. (a) Verify one eigenpair directly, say λ=6\lambda=6λ=6. (b) Confirm the three eigenvectors are mutually orthogonal. (c) Normalise them to build an orthogonal matrix Q\mathbf{Q}Q and write the spectral decomposition A=QDQT\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{Q}^{\mathsf{T}}A=QDQT.
hints: For (a) you need only one matrix–vector multiplication: apply A\mathbf{A}A to the stated eigenvector and check the result is 666 times it.
For (b) take the three pairwise dot products. They must all vanish — guaranteed here, since a symmetric matrix with distinct eigenvalues always has orthogonal eigenvectors.

For (c) divide each eigenvector by its own length to make the columns of Q\mathbf{Q}Q orthonormal; then Q−1=QT\mathbf{Q}^{-1}=\mathbf{Q}^{\mathsf{T}}Q−1=QT. The box wants those three lengths, in the order the eigenvectors are listed.
problems.format: the three eigenvectors' lengths, 3 d.p., in order

problems.html: Show that A=(5−113)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}5&-1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}A=(51​−13​) is not diagonalisable.
hints: Start as usual with the characteristic equation and see what is unusual about its roots.
Expanding (5−λ)(3−λ)+1(5-\lambda)(3-\lambda)+1(5−λ)(3−λ)+1 gives a quadratic that is a perfect square — a repeated eigenvalue. That alone does not settle it.

Now count independent eigenvectors: at your repeated root, solve (A−λI)v=0(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}(A−λI)v=0 and count the free unknowns. One eigenvector for a doubled eigenvalue means defective; the box wants that doubled eigenvalue.

problems.html: A streaming service tracks subscribers. Each month a subscribed user stays subscribed with probability 0.80.80.8 and lapses with 0.20.20.2; a lapsed user resubscribes with 0.40.40.4 and stays lapsed with 0.60.60.6. Let xn=(subscribed, lapsed)\mathbf{x}_n=(\text{subscribed},\,\text{lapsed})xn​=(subscribed,lapsed) fractions. (a) Write the transition matrix P\mathbf{P}P and find its eigenvalues; (b) find the steady-state distribution; (c) starting from everyone subscribed, x0=(1,0)\mathbf{x}_0=(1,0)x0​=(1,0), find a closed form for xn\mathbf{x}_nxn​ and state the long-run subscribed fraction.
hints: Build P\mathbf{P}P so that each column describes where one state goes next — the columns, not the rows, must sum to 111.
Every transition matrix has one eigenvalue you can name without any algebra, because its columns sum to 111; find the other from the trace, since the two eigenvalues sum to it.

For (c), decompose x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​ in the eigenbasis: the second eigenvalue's contribution decays like its nnn-th power, which is exactly why the chain settles. For the box, the steady state is the eigenvector for the eigenvalue you named, scaled so its entries sum to 111.
problems.format: eigenvalues as decimals; steady state, exact

problems.html: Let A=(1−221)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}A=(12​−21​) and xn+1=Axn\mathbf{x}_{n+1}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_nxn+1​=Axn​. (a) Find the eigenvalues of A\mathbf{A}A and an eigenvector. (b) Starting from x0=(1,0)T\mathbf{x}_0=(1,0)^{\mathsf{T}}x0​=(1,0)T, compute x1,x2,x3\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2,\mathbf{x}_3x1​,x2​,x3​, plot the four points and sketch the orbit through them. (c) Relate what you draw to the modulus and argument of the eigenvalues.
hints: The characteristic equation is (1−λ)2+4=0(1-\lambda)^2+4=0(1−λ)2+4=0, which has no real solution: expect a complex conjugate pair.
For (b) just multiply: apply A\mathbf{A}A to x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​, then to the result, and again.
For (c) compute ∣λ∣=a2+b2|\lambda|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}∣λ∣=a2+b2​ and compare the lengths of your points: each step should multiply the length by the same factor.
problems.format: x₃'s two entries; then |λ| to 3 d.p.

problems.html:
State whether each is true or false, with a one-line justification.

  1. Every real 2×22\times22×2 matrix has at least one real eigenvalue.

  2. If A\mathbf{A}A is invertible, 000 is not an eigenvalue of A\mathbf{A}A.

  3. A 3×33\times33×3 matrix with eigenvalues 2,2,52,2,52,2,5 can never be diagonalised.

  4. Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent.

  5. A real symmetric matrix can have a non-real eigenvalue.

  6. If λ\lambdaλ is an eigenvalue of A\mathbf{A}A, then λ2\lambda^2λ2 is an eigenvalue of A2\mathbf{A}^2A2.
hints: A universal claim falls to a single counterexample. For (a), test it on the quarter-turn (0−110)\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}(01​−10​): what are its eigenvalues? Weigh the others one at a time.
For (b), write out what λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 means in Av=λv\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}Av=λv with v≠0\mathbf{v}\neq\mathbf{0}v=0, then compare it with what invertible means.

For (c), a repeated eigenvalue only blocks diagonalisation when its eigenspace is too small, and "never" is a universal claim: look for a 3×33\times33×3 with eigenvalues 2,2,52,2,52,2,5 whose λ=2\lambda=2λ=2 has two free unknowns (diagonal matrices are the easiest place to look). For (e), remember what the spectral theorem guarantees about symmetric matrices.

problems.html: Show that a real symmetric matrix A=(abbd)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&d\end{pmatrix}A=(ab​bd​) always has real eigenvalues. (This is the 2×22\times22×2 case of the spectral theorem that underpins the orthogonal diagonalisation in Exercise 2.5.)
hints: Write the characteristic equation for the general symmetric (abbd)\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&d\end{pmatrix}(ab​bd​) and get it into the form λ2−(a+d)λ+(ad−b2)=0\lambda^2-(a+d)\lambda+(ad-b^2)=0λ2−(a+d)λ+(ad−b2)=0.
Real roots are exactly the condition that the discriminant is ≥0\geq 0≥0. Compute it.

Expand the discriminant: a2+2ad+d2−4ad+4b2a^2+2ad+d^2-4ad+4b^2a2+2ad+d2−4ad+4b2. Collect the aaa and ddd terms into a single square, then say why what is left can never be negative. For the box, put a=1a=1a=1, b=2b=2b=2, d=3d=3d=3 into the discriminant.
problems.format: the discriminant when a = 1, b = 2, d = 3

problems.html: For each matrix find the eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each (allow complex values, and note any defective case): (a) (2−112),(b) (1−113).\text{(a)}\ \begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}.(a) (21​−12​),(b) (11​−13​).
hints: Form det⁡(A−λI)=0\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0det(A−λI)=0 in each case; the trace and determinant give a quick check on the roots.
In (a) the discriminant is negative, so expect a complex conjugate pair: carry on regardless, the method is unchanged.

In (b) the characteristic polynomial is a perfect square. A repeated root is not the end of the story: solve (A−λI)v=0(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}(A−λI)v=0 at that root and count the free unknowns. The box wants only the root itself.
problems.format: (a) as a+bi, +i first; then the λ of (b)

problems.html: Find all eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each of A=(120210004)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\2&1&0\\0&0&4\end{pmatrix}A=​120​210​004​​.
hints: Notice the block structure: the third row and column are isolated. Expand det⁡(A−λI)\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})det(A−λI) along the third row and one linear factor drops out at once.
That leaves the 2×22\times22×2 block (1221)\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}(12​21​) to handle on its own.
Its characteristic equation is (1−λ)2−4=0(1-\lambda)^2-4=0(1−λ)2−4=0.

problems.html: Let A=(0121)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\2&1\end{pmatrix}A=(02​11​). Diagonalise it and find a closed form for An\mathbf{A}^{n}An.
hints: Characteristic equation: λ2−λ−2=0\lambda^2-\lambda-2=0λ2−λ−2=0.
Factorise it, then find an eigenvector for each root to build P\mathbf{P}P.

The problem finishes with An=PDnP−1\mathbf{A}^n=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}An=PDnP−1, but the box wants only the eigenvalues: check that they add to tr⁡A\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{A}trA and multiply to det⁡A\det\mathbf{A}detA.

problems.html: Let H=(41+i1−i3)\mathbf{H}=\begin{pmatrix}4&1+\mathrm{i}\\1-\mathrm{i}&3\end{pmatrix}H=(41−i​1+i3​). Check it is Hermitian, find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and verify the eigenvectors are orthogonal under the conjugate inner product. What would the plain product uTv\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{v}uTv have said?
hints: Check the Hermitian property first: conjugate every entry, transpose, and compare with the original.
For the eigenvalues use (1+i)(1−i)=2(1+\mathrm{i})(1-\mathrm{i})=2(1+i)(1−i)=2, so the characteristic equation is (4−λ)(3−λ)−2=0(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2=0(4−λ)(3−λ)−2=0.

For the orthogonality check, conjugate the first vector's entries before multiplying; the plain product skips that. For the box, read the eigenvector for the larger eigenvalue off the first row of H−λI\mathbf{H}-\lambda\mathbf{I}H−λI, taking v2=1v_2=1v2​=1.
problems.format: λs smaller first; then v₁ for λ=5 when v₂=1

problems.html: For each matrix, give the algebraic and geometric multiplicity of every eigenvalue, and say whether it is diagonalisable: (a) (210020003),(b) (200020003),(c) (4201).\text{(a)}\ \begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \begin{pmatrix}4&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.(a) ​200​120​003​​,(b) ​200​020​003​​,(c) (40​21​).
hints: Algebraic multiplicity counts how often an eigenvalue repeats as a root; geometric multiplicity counts its independent eigenvectors.
The geometric multiplicity is the number of free unknowns when you solve (A−λI)v=0(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}(A−λI)v=0.

A matrix is diagonalisable exactly when the two multiplicities agree for every eigenvalue. (a) and (b) share their eigenvalues and algebraic multiplicities, so only the count of free unknowns can tell them apart.

problems.html: A data set has (scaled) covariance matrix A=(4221)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}A=(42​21​). (a) Find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors. (b) Confirm the eigenvectors are orthogonal. (c) In PCA terms, along which direction does the data vary, and how much variance lies in the perpendicular direction?
hints: Set up det⁡(A−λI)=0\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0det(A−λI)=0 and expand carefully — the constant term is what matters here.
The determinant is (4−λ)(1−λ)−4(4-\lambda)(1-\lambda)-4(4−λ)(1−λ)−4. Expand it and collect like terms; the quadratic you get solves by taking out a common factor.

For (c), each eigenvalue is the variance along its eigenvector: what does the smaller one say about the spread perpendicular to the main axis? For the box, check your two eigenvalues against tr⁡A\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{A}trA and det⁡A\det\mathbf{A}detA.

problems.html: The symmetric matrix A=(320242025)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}3&2&0\\2&4&2\\0&2&5\end{pmatrix}A=​320​242​025​​ (think of it as a covariance matrix) has eigenvalues λ=1,4,7\lambda=1,4,7λ=1,4,7, with eigenvectors (2,−2,1)T(2,-2,1)^{\mathsf{T}}(2,−2,1)T, (2,1,−2)T(2,1,-2)^{\mathsf{T}}(2,1,−2)T, (1,2,2)T(1,2,2)^{\mathsf{T}}(1,2,2)T respectively. (As in Exercise 2.5, the eigenvectors are supplied so the work stays clean.) (a) Verify one eigenpair directly, say λ=7\lambda=7λ=7. (b) Confirm the three eigenvectors are mutually orthogonal. (c) Normalise them to build an orthogonal matrix Q\mathbf{Q}Q and write the spectral decomposition A=QDQT\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{Q}^{\mathsf{T}}A=QDQT. (d) In PCA language, which direction is the first principal axis and what fraction of the total variance does it carry?
hints: For (a) apply A\mathbf{A}A to the stated eigenvector and check you get 777 times it back: one multiplication settles it.

For (c) normalise each eigenvector by dividing by its own length, so that Q\mathbf{Q}Q has orthonormal columns and Q−1=QT\mathbf{Q}^{-1}=\mathbf{Q}^{\mathsf{T}}Q−1=QT. All three lengths are the same here.
For (d) the first principal axis is the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue, and the variance it carries is that eigenvalue as a fraction of the total, which is the trace.
problems.format: the fraction of the variance on the first axis

problems.html: A regular Markov chain settles to a unique steady state when λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 occurs just once and every other eigenvalue has modulus less than 111. For each transition matrix, find the eigenvalues and say whether the chain converges or oscillates: (a) P=(0.70.20.30.8),(b) P=(0110).\text{(a)}\ \mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix}0.7&0.2\\0.3&0.8\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.(a) P=(0.70.3​0.20.8​),(b) P=(01​10​). (c) For the chain in (a), starting from x0=(1,0)\mathbf{x}_0=(1,0)x0​=(1,0), find a closed form for xn\mathbf{x}_nxn​ and its limit.
hints: Find both eigenvalues in each case; every transition matrix has λ=1\lambda=1λ=1, so the trace hands you the other one. Then compare the second eigenvalue's modulus with 111.
For (c), find the steady state and the eigenvector of the second eigenvalue, then write x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​ as a combination of the two.

The steady state sums to 111 and the other eigenvector sums to 000, so the steady state's coefficient is 111. Each term is then scaled by its eigenvalue to the nnn; put n=3n=3n=3 and read off the first entry.

questions.stem: A 2×22\times22×2 matrix has the repeated eigenvalue λ=4\lambda=4λ=4. Is it diagonalisable?
options: Yes — every square matrix with a real eigenvalue is diagonalisable.
Yes, provided the matrix is invertible.
No — a repeated eigenvalue always blocks diagonalisation.
Not enough information: it depends on how many independent eigenvectors λ=4\lambda=4λ=4 has.
questions.hint: The repeated eigenvalue is only half the story. Compare 4I4\mathbf{I}4I with (4104)\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\0&4\end{pmatrix}(40​14​) — both have λ=4\lambda=4λ=4 twice.
questions.why: A repeated eigenvalue is a warning, not a verdict. What matters is the geometric multiplicity — the number of independent eigenvectors, which is the nullity of A−4I\mathbf{A}-4\mathbf{I}A−4I. If that is 222 the matrix is diagonalisable (indeed A=4I\mathbf{A}=4\mathbf{I}A=4I); if it is 111 the matrix is defective. Invertibility is irrelevant: (4104)\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\0&4\end{pmatrix}(40​14​) is invertible and not diagonalisable.

questions.stem: The rotation R=(0−110)\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}R=(01​−10​) has eigenvalues ±i\pm\mathrm{i}±i. What does having no real eigenvalue mean geometrically?
options: The rotation must be by more than 180∘180^\circ180∘.
The matrix is singular, so it collapses the plane to a line.
No real direction is preserved — every vector is genuinely turned.
The matrix has no eigenvectors of any kind.
questions.hint: A real eigenvector would be a direction the map merely stretches. Picture a quarter-turn of the plane and try to find one.
questions.why: A real eigenvector would be a direction the map merely stretches. A quarter-turn moves every direction, so no such real direction exists — which is exactly what a complex-conjugate pair of eigenvalues records. The matrix is not singular (det⁡R=1\det\mathbf{R}=1detR=1), and it does have eigenvectors: they simply live in C2\mathbb{C}^2C2 rather than R2\mathbb{R}^2R2.

questions.stem: Why is v=0\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}v=0 excluded from the definition of an eigenvector?
options: Because eigenvalues must be non-zero.
Because A0=λ0\mathbf{A}\mathbf{0}=\lambda\mathbf{0}A0=λ0 holds for every λ\lambdaλ, so it would tell us nothing.
Because the zero vector has no length.
Because A0\mathbf{A}\mathbf{0}A0 is undefined.
questions.hint: Put v=0\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}v=0 into Av=λv\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}Av=λv and ask which values of λ\lambdaλ satisfy it.
questions.why: A0=0=λ0\mathbf{A}\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}=\lambda\mathbf{0}A0=0=λ0 is true for every scalar λ\lambdaλ whatsoever. Admitting 0\mathbf{0}0 would make every number an eigenvalue of every matrix, and the definition would carry no information. Note that eigenvalues themselves may perfectly well be zero — that happens exactly when A\mathbf{A}A is singular.

questions.stem: You compute eigenvalues λ1=3, λ2=5\lambda_1=3,\ \lambda_2=5λ1​=3, λ2​=5 for a matrix with trace 999. What should you conclude?
options: Nothing is wrong; the trace is unrelated to the eigenvalues.
There is an arithmetic error: the eigenvalues must sum to the trace.
The matrix is not diagonalisable.
The remaining eigenvalue must be 111.
questions.hint: There is a one-line check relating the eigenvalues to the trace. Add the two you have.
questions.why: For an n×nn\times nn×n matrix the eigenvalues sum to the trace and multiply to the determinant. Here 3+5=8≠93+5=8\neq93+5=8=9, so something has gone wrong — most often a sign slip in expanding det⁡(A−λI)\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})det(A−λI). This is the cheapest check available and is worth doing every single time.

questions.stem: In a diagonalisation A=PDP−1\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{P}^{-1}A=PDP−1, what must be true of the order of the columns of P\mathbf{P}P?
options: They must be in increasing order of eigenvalue.
They must be normalised to unit length.
The order does not matter at all.
The order is free, but must match the order of the eigenvalues down D\mathbf{D}D.
questions.hint: Multiply out AP=PD\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}AP=PD and read what it says one column at a time.
questions.why: Any ordering of the eigenvectors gives a valid diagonalisation, but the kkk-th column of P\mathbf{P}P must be an eigenvector for the kkk-th diagonal entry of D\mathbf{D}D. Swapping one without the other breaks the identity. Normalising is optional for diagonalisation in general — it matters for the orthogonal diagonalisation of a symmetric matrix, where P−1=PT\mathbf{P}^{-1}=\mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}}P−1=PT requires orthonormal columns.

questions.stem: A Markov chain's transition matrix always has λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 as an eigenvalue. What does the corresponding eigenvector represent?
options: A distribution left unchanged by one step — the steady state.
The starting distribution of the chain.
The fastest-decaying mode of the chain.
The direction in which the chain grows without bound.
questions.hint: Write out what Pv=1⋅v\mathbf{P}\mathbf{v}=1\cdot\mathbf{v}Pv=1⋅v says about applying one step of the chain to v\mathbf{v}v.
questions.why: Pv=1⋅v\mathbf{P}\mathbf{v}=1\cdot\mathbf{v}Pv=1⋅v says precisely that applying one step leaves v\mathbf{v}v unchanged, which is what a steady state is. Scaled so its entries sum to 111, it is the long-run distribution. Nothing grows without bound: the other eigenvalues have modulus below 111 for a regular chain, so their contributions die away and the λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 direction is what survives.

questions.stem: S\mathbf{S}S is a real symmetric matrix. What does that guarantee about its eigenvalues?
options: They are all real.
They are all real, and always distinct.
They may be complex, as for a rotation.
They are all real and positive.
questions.hint: Three different claims are being run together here: real, positive, and distinct. Symmetry buys exactly one of them — try to break the other two with a small example.
questions.why: A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues, and eigenvectors belonging to different eigenvalues are orthogonal. That is all symmetry gives, and the two overreaches are easy to break. Positivity fails for (0110)\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}(01​10​), which is symmetric with eigenvalues ±1\pm1±1; positivity is a further condition, called positive definiteness. Distinctness fails for the identity, symmetric with the eigenvalue 111 twice. Complex eigenvalues genuinely do occur — the rotation of this unit has ±i\pm\mathrm{i}±i — but a rotation is not symmetric, which is exactly why it is allowed them.

questions.stem: For complex vectors, orthogonality is tested with u†v=u1‾v1+u2‾v2\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{v}=\overline{u_{1}}v_{1}+\overline{u_{2}}v_{2}u†v=u1​​v1​+u2​​v2​ rather than u1v1+u2v2u_{1}v_{1}+u_{2}v_{2}u1​v1​+u2​v2​. Why the conjugate?
options: Because the conjugate makes every inner product real.
Without it, u†u\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{u}u†u need not be a positive real number, so it could not measure a length.
It is only a convention; the two tests agree in every case.
Because a complex matrix is never symmetric.
questions.hint: Try both versions on the single vector u=(1,i)\mathbf{u}=(1,\mathrm{i})u=(1,i), and ask which one returns a sensible squared length.
questions.why: Take u=(1,i)\mathbf{u}=(1,\mathrm{i})u=(1,i). Without the conjugate, 1⋅1+i⋅i=1−1=01\cdot1+\mathrm{i}\cdot\mathrm{i}=1-1=01⋅1+i⋅i=1−1=0, so a perfectly good non-zero vector would come out with zero length and be orthogonal to itself. With the conjugate, ∣1∣2+∣i∣2=2\left|1\right|^{2}+\left|\mathrm{i}\right|^{2}=2∣1∣2+∣i∣2=2, which is what a squared length should look like — and the pattern echoes ∣z∣2=z‾z\left|z\right|^{2}=\overline{z}z∣z∣2=zz from Unit 3. So the two tests certainly do not agree. Complex symmetric matrices exist; the useful class here is the Hermitian one, A†=A\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}=\mathbf{A}A†=A. And u†v\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{v}u†v is not real in general — it satisfies u†v=v†u‾\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{v}=\overline{\mathbf{v}^{\dagger}\mathbf{u}}u†v=v†u, which forces only u†u\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{u}u†u to be real.

questions.stem: Av=3v\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=3\mathbf{v}Av=3v for some non-zero v\mathbf{v}v. What is A2v\mathbf{A}^{2}\mathbf{v}A2v?
options: 9v9\mathbf{v}9v
3v3\mathbf{v}3v
6v6\mathbf{v}6v
It cannot be determined without knowing A\mathbf{A}A itself.
questions.hint: Apply A\mathbf{A}A twice, one step at a time, using what you are told at each step.
questions.why: Apply A\mathbf{A}A twice: A2v=A(Av)=A(3v)=3(Av)=3⋅3v=9v\mathbf{A}^{2}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{A}(3\mathbf{v})=3(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v})=3\cdot3\mathbf{v}=9\mathbf{v}A2v=A(Av)=A(3v)=3(Av)=3⋅3v=9v. The eigenvector goes through untouched and only the eigenvalue is transformed — squaring the matrix squares the eigenvalue. The same one-eigenvector-at-a-time reading gives A−1v=13v\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{v}=\tfrac13\mathbf{v}A−1v=31​v and (A+kI)v=(3+k)v(\mathbf{A}+k\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=(3+k)\mathbf{v}(A+kI)v=(3+k)v: powers, shifts and inverses all keep the eigenvectors, which is what makes diagonalisation worth the trouble. Doubling would be the answer to 2Av2\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}2Av, a different question, and no further knowledge of A\mathbf{A}A is needed.
